description: I’m Griffin, the solo creator of the RAC Space team, named in honor of my grandfather's initials, who was a propulsion engineer at NASA. I'm interested in software development, engineering, and space exploration. RAC Space brings those interests together while honoring his work and the inspiration he continues to give me.
summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web app for exploring how location and time affect sunlight and Earth visibility on the Moon. 

Users can search named features or select coordinates on a 3D Moon. The app calculates terrain obstruction, compares saved sites over a chosen date range, and highlights sampled locations where sunlight and a view toward Earth coincide. Horizon charts, calendars, and  solar power estimation help explain the trade offs.
details:
What it does

Lunar Landing Site Navigator estimates sunlight and Earth visibility at locations on the Moon. It uses NASA terrain data and calculated Sun and Earth positions to check whether the surrounding landscape blocks the view, then compares those conditions across sites and dates.

How the calculations work

  1. Prepare the terrain. NASA LRO LOLA elevation data is converted into terrain tiles. These tiles build the 3D Moon and provide the surface heights used in the visibility calculations. More detail loads as the viewer zooms in.
  2. Sample the location. A point is checked at one location. A circular region is checked at a grid of locations within its boundary. Each sample uses the local terrain height so the calculation starts on the Moon's surface.
  3. Locate the Sun and Earth. NASA/JPL SPICE calculates their positions relative to each surface sample at the requested time. The app uses these positions to determine their direction and height above the local horizon. JPL Horizons provides reference checks for Earth's calculated direction.
  4. Check what the terrain blocks. Open3D traces lines from each sample toward different parts of the Sun and Earth. The share of clear lines estimates how much of each body is visible, including partial obstruction. Earth also has a separate check for a clear line toward its center.
  5. Reuse the terrain calculations. Saved horizon profiles describe the surrounding skyline. They let later calculations reuse known clear or blocked directions. Directions that remain uncertain are checked against the terrain directly.
  6. Repeat across the plan. The app runs these checks at regular intervals between the plan's start and end times. Background workers save results as they finish. Completed results and terrain preparations are reused, so a stopped plan can continue without starting over.
  7. Combine sunlight and Earth visibility. At each sampled location and time, the app checks for visible sunlight above a small cutoff and a clear line toward Earth's center. It estimates how long these conditions overlap across the plan and marks the best sampled locations, including ties.
  8. Build the result views. Saved results feed the calendars, terrain maps, summaries, and horizon charts. A shared time selection keeps the views aligned. The time finder searches those results for times that meet selected visibility minimums.
  9. Estimate solar output and export. The solar estimate combines visible sunlight, Sun elevation, panel area, and panel efficiency. It compares a level panel with ideal Sun tracking. Results can also be exported as CSV for further inspection.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Compare nearby sites and alternative schedules for preliminary lunar planning.
  • Find sampled periods when sunlight and Earth visibility overlap, including when a schedule changes.
  • Make the effects of terrain, timing, and solar panel orientation easier to understand through maps and charts.

Design and creative approach

The creative approach is bringing these scenarios into one connected workflow, where the terrain, selected time, and Sun/Earth results stay linked as users compare locations and schedules.

  • Compare landing options: Check nearby points or regions to see how surrounding terrain changes sunlight and Earth visibility.
  • Explore schedule changes: Run the same sites over different date ranges to understand how a delayed or shifted mission could change conditions.
  • Find overlapping conditions: Identify sampled locations and times where sunlight and a clear view toward Earth occur together.
  • Explore power trade-offs: Compare a level solar panel with ideal Sun tracking to illustrate how Sun elevation affects estimated output.
  • Support learning: Connect the 3D landscape, horizon chart, and timeline so users can understand why conditions change.

Tools and development

  • Frontend: Vue 3, TypeScript, Three.js, Pinia, and Vue Router.
  • Backend and calculations: Python, Django, Django REST Framework, SpiceyPy, NumPy, Rasterio, and Open3D.
  • Background jobs and storage: Celery and Redis run jobs. SQLite stores terrain tiles, saved horizons, sites, plans, and results.
  • Local setup and verification: Docker Compose, repository setup instructions, and automated tests.

Factors considered and limitations

  • Terrain detail: Features missing from the imported elevation data cannot cast calculated shadows.
  • Sampling: Results describe the places and times checked. Conditions between samples and exact rise/set times are not calculated.
  • Time and missing results: All times are UTC. Area averages are separate from center-point results. Missing results stay unavailable rather than counting as darkness or a blocked Earth view.
  • Earth visibility: A clear line of sight does not establish a working radio connection. Antennas, ground stations, radio link budgets, and relay satellites are not modeled.
  • Solar estimate: Uses a fixed sunlight reference and simplified panel assumptions. Battery storage, temperature, dust, electrical losses, and eclipses are not included.
  • Intended use: An exploration prototype that has not been validated for landing safety. Horizons reference checks cover Earth's direction, not the accuracy of terrain shadows.

AI assistance

  • AI-assisted development: AI assisted with coding, debugging, data integration, calculation logic, documentation, and preparing project materials.
  • Disclosure: See the AI use document in the project repository for the general use cases.
